name: Aaron Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the respiratory ward at Eastgate General. It's chest infections, people with COPD, which is long-term lung disease, and a few on non-invasive ventilation, the tight masks that push air in. Twelve-hour shifts, mostly days. On top of that I do bank shifts, which are extra shifts through the hospital's own staff pool, usually two Saturdays a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the respiratory side because you see results fast. Someone comes in grey and gasping and three days later they're arguing with you about the food. What wears me out is the hours. The bank shifts aren't optional for me. My dad died two years ago and I help pay my mother's rent, and my younger sister Hana's at university. I live alone in a studio flat, and I've got about two weeks' money in the bank at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. That's not hard to picture, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably for the best, at least for now. I'd tell people at work we were right to be a bit sceptical, but some of the tools were useful. I'm not one for big statements online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me AI was never the issue. The issue is the hospital's budget. My mother's rent is paid by my bank shifts on Saturdays. When the hospital cuts bank shifts, she feels it before I do. And they've already said bank will be cut next year to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my normal shifts and try to get on the list for bank shifts at the private chest clinic across town, which pays a bit more. I'd stop eating at the hospital canteen and take food from home. I'd ask Hana to look for a weekend job, which I've been putting off because I want her to focus on her studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired and a bit trapped. It's not AI, it's the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother if bank shifts were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at first. I'd find the money somewhere else before I told her. She'd worry, and she'd try to work again, and her knees are bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine part of your job you'd be glad AI took, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The oxygen prescription charts. We redo them every time the doctor changes the target, by hand. If something did that automatically, I'd take it.

say: I'd say a **sceptical** approach was right, though some tools were useful.
I'd avoid **big statements** online and keep it to work chat.
think: The **hospital budget**, not AI, is what threatens my income.
My **bank shifts** pay my mother's rent, and they're due to be cut next year.
do: Keep normal shifts and join the **private chest clinic** bank list.
Stop eating at the **canteen** and bring food from home.
Ask his sister to find a **weekend job** at university.
feel: **Tired** and a bit **trapped** by money, not by AI.
S0.quote: My mother's rent is paid by my bank shifts on Saturdays. When the hospital cuts bank shifts, she feels it before I do.
fieldNote: His income is **already at risk** from planned bank cuts, so even the calmest picture worries him.

He'd hide money trouble from his **mother** to protect her health.

steps.text: Keep his normal shifts on the respiratory ward
Join the bank list at the private chest clinic across town
Take food from home instead of using the canteen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what's already starting, to be honest. The rota system's changing next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mixed bag. Good if it cuts the paperwork, bad if it's used to squeeze staff. I'd probably share a sensible article or two with the team, nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota is the bit that worries me. If an AI rota can fill the gaps on paper, nobody needs a nurse like me picking up extra Saturdays. My main job's probably fine, it's hands-on, but my extra money is the first thing a smart system would cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the new rota app once a few people said it worked, and learn how to put myself forward for shifts on it before others do. I'd apply for the ventilation course, the one that gets you signed off on the masks, because specialist skills get picked first. And I'd try to put 50 a month aside, even if that means fewer trips home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot of worry about money. My job feels okay, my income doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, he's the charge nurse I trust. He'd tell me straight whether the bank shifts are going. Then I'd call Hana, not my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take the course. What does it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital pays the fee, but I'd lose two Saturdays of bank shifts to study days. That's money my mother doesn't get that month. It's worth it, but it stings.

I'd share **sensible articles** with the team, nothing angry.

S1.quote: If an AI rota can fill the gaps on paper, nobody needs a nurse like me picking up extra Saturdays.
fieldNote: He separates his **job**, which feels safe, from his **income**, which doesn't.

steps.text: Learn the new rota app early to get first pick of shifts
Apply for the hospital's non-invasive ventilation course
Save 50 a month by making fewer trips home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots by 2031. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in with a plan, and quickly. Something sensible, help with retraining, not panic. I'd say nurses will be needed for a while yet, because the robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking parts of my job, the charts, the obs, the oxygen calculations, go by 2028. Then the hands-on side starts going in 2031. Two years is enough to learn intensive care, not enough to save. I'd be choosing between a course and my mother's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the intensive care course straight away, because critical care will need people longest. I'd sit down with Hana and my uncle and split my mother's rent three ways, which we've never done. I'd cut my phone to the cheapest plan and sell my bike. And I'd keep every bank shift I can until they disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when a patient's oxygen starts dropping and you know you've got minutes, not hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for a respiratory nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years where I'm still needed for hands, the masks, the positioning, the suctioning. But the bank shifts would go in 2028, because a system can plan staff perfectly. So my main pay survives a bit longer, my extra pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think of leaving nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in two years, there's nowhere to go round here that's safer. Most jobs in town are warehouse or call centre, and the card says those go too. I'd stay and get as specialist as I can.

I'd say nurses are still needed for a while because **robots come later**.

feel: **Alarmed**, like a patient's oxygen dropping with minutes to act.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to learn intensive care, not enough to save. I'd be choosing between a course and my mother's rent.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose a big part** of his income in 2028 when bank shifts vanish.
Asking family to **share the rent** is a first, and a hard step for him.
He sees **no safer jobs** in town, so he digs into specialist nursing.

steps.text: Apply for the intensive care course straight away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, 2031, then robots around 2034. That gives me a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly. Retraining, sensible rules, nurses involved. Nothing dramatic, just a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd learn the breathing machines inside out, because robots will struggle with a panicking patient on a mask. I'd be 32 at the AGI part and 35 for the robots. If I'm a specialist by then, I'm probably all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ventilation course in year one, then intensive care in year two or three. I'd get better with the AI tools once they're proven on the ward, so I'm not the one left behind. I'd try to save 80 a month and get three months' money behind me by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but working on it. It feels like a long shift with a good team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your mother and sister in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana graduates in two years, so by 2028 she's earning and can help with the rent. That changes everything. Five years means I'm not carrying them alone the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold off on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving out of the studio. I'd love a proper flat, but that would wait. Savings first.

I'd keep it **calm**, with nothing dramatic.

Use **AI tools** on the ward once they're proven.

S3.quote: With five years I'd learn the breathing machines inside out, because robots will struggle with a panicking patient on a mask.
fieldNote: His sister **graduating** by 2028 is the real turning point for the household.

steps.text: Take the ventilation course in year one, then intensive care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and robots around 2039. I'd be 37 and 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a reasonable time to adjust, as long as people use it. I'd tell the younger nurses to get a specialism. That's the advice I'd give anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to stop sending money home and start building something of my own. That's the part that scares me, not the AI. I've been looking after other people since I was 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the ventilation course and then intensive care, at a normal pace. I'd keep my bank shifts as long as they last. Once Hana's working, I'd move the rent money into a savings account in my own name, which feels strange to even say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy about money, not about the future. It's an odd kind of relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do with savings of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fix my teeth, honestly. I've had a cracked molar for a year. Then a deposit on a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you think about leaving the respiratory ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for intensive care, which is the same family of work. I wouldn't leave nursing. I'd just move deeper into it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The bank shifts go first, and those are my mother's rent. What would help is the hospital keeping a fair share of shifts for staff, not letting a system squeeze them out, and some help with family costs for people like me. Nobody counts the people a nurse's wage is feeding. Mine feeds three, and only one of them is me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people we support outside work. Your questions assume it's just me and a partner. For a lot of nurses it's parents, siblings, sometimes people back home.

headlineQuote: Nobody counts the people a nurse's wage is feeding. Mine feeds three, and only one of them is me.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old respiratory nurse** who lives alone in a studio flat.
His **bank shifts** pay his widowed mother's rent, and his sister is at university.
He's **anxious** even in the calm picture, because the hospital plans to cut bank shifts.
Fast AGI makes him **alarmed**, expecting his extra income to vanish in 2028.
He answers every picture by going **deeper** into specialist nursing, never out of it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his bank shifts and his mother's rent would go first.
whatWouldHelp: The hospital keeping **bank shifts** for staff rather than letting software squeeze them.
Some help with **family costs** for nurses who support relatives.
